node.label: Joel Mokyr
node.date_label: “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” 1977 · The Lever of Riches 1990 · editor’s introduction, The British Industrial Revolution 1999 · The Gifts of Athena 2002 · Max Weber Lecture on the European Enlightenment 2007 · The Enlightened Economy 2009 · with Kelly and Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” 2014 · A Culture of Growth 2016 · “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” 2023 · with Tabellini, “Why China and Europe Diverged” 2023 · economics prize 2025
node.description: An economic historian of technology at Northwestern University who explained sustained growth by the growth of “useful knowledge”. In 1977 he judged demand factors “of a secondary order of importance” in the Industrial Revolution. His 1999 introduction defended the term against the charge that it was “a concept too many” and defined the Industrial Revolution as “a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions”. Two drafts of 2002, which say they adapt The Gifts of Athena (2002; unread here, though its reviewer Zorina Khan reports the same scheme), divided useful knowledge into “propositional” knowledge of natural regularities and “prescriptive” instructions (February), and called the Enlightenment’s contribution “the Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention”, finding Pomeranz’s coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself” unable to explain the gap (October). In a 2007 lecture the Enlightenment kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out”. Reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), C. Knick Harley wondered whether “causation from Enlightenment … to economic change actually existed”, while finding that the book made “a strong case” that “the history of ideas and their place in society needs to be at the core of the story” (2010). In Claude Diebolt’s account of A Culture of Growth (2016), culture works “as the invisible hand”, in a phenomenon “related to an elite” of philosophers, scientists, engineers, instrument makers and industrialists; Diebolt regretted “the lack of in-depth consideration of the German language literature” (2017). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda he answered Robert Allen’s high-wage explanation with British workers’ human capital (2014), and found that across England’s 41 counties industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023). With Guido Tabellini he traced China’s and Europe’s political divergence to clans and corporations (2023). In 2025 he was awarded a share of the economics prize in memory of Alfred Nobel, cited “for having identified the prerequisites for sustained growth through technological progress”.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Joel Mokyr (b. 1946); Industrialization in the Low Countries, 1795–1850 (1976); “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” (Journal of Economic History, 1977); The Lever of Riches (1990); “Editor’s Introduction: The New Economic History and the Industrial Revolution” (1999); The Gifts of Athena: Historical Origins of the Knowledge Economy (2002); The European Enlightenment, the Industrial Revolution, and Modern Economic Growth (Max Weber Lecture, 2007); The Enlightened Economy: An Economic History of Britain 1700–1850 (2009); with Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014) and “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (2023); A Culture of Growth (2016); with Guido Tabellini, “Social Organizations and Political Institutions: Why China and Europe Diverged” (Economica, 2023–24); with Avner Greif and Guido Tabellini, Two Paths to Prosperity (2025). Readers: B. Zorina Khan (2003); C. Knick Harley (2010); Claude Diebolt (2017); the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (2025).
node.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-18 in his own words: the 1977 article’s abstract (Cambridge Core); the 1999 editor’s introduction (author-posted manuscript, pp. 1–2, 14, 16); two 2002 drafts posted on his Northwestern site, “Useful Knowledge as an Evolving System” (February, pp. 1–7) and “The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle” (October, pp. 1–4, 10), each adapted, he says, from The Gifts of Athena; the 2007 Max Weber Lecture (pp. 1–5, 13, 16–17); “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.1–16.4); “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (2023, pp. 59–61); and the 2023 manuscript with Tabellini (abstract and pp. 1–3). His books are unread: The Gifts of Athena is known through Khan’s review (2003), The Enlightened Economy through Harley’s (2010) and A Culture of Growth through Diebolt’s (2017); The Lever of Riches, the 1976 book and Two Paths to Prosperity (2025, with Greif and Tabellini) are dated from metadata only. Each quotation is attributed to the text it comes from; the 2002 drafts’ wording is not claimed for the later books. The October 2002 draft was written for a November conference; its delivery is not asserted. The 2023 findings with Kelly and Ó Gráda concern differences across English counties, not Britain’s international position. The prize motivation is quoted from the Royal Swedish Academy’s press release of 13 October 2025, which dates the announcement, not the ceremony. Harley’s and Diebolt’s accounts of the books they reviewed are attributed to them. His explanation is one of several in the debate entry capitalismdebates, beside Wrigley’s, de Vries’s and Allen’s; his invention–adoption distinction stays on technology/invention_adoption.

incident_edges.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

incident_edges.relationship: Useful knowledge and the epistemic base of technique: propositional and prescriptive knowledge, macro- and microinventions, and stasis where techniques rest on “narrow epistemic bases” (1999, 2002)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. Editor’s introduction (1999, author-posted manuscript): “a successful macroinvention meets three criteria: novelty, workability, and potential for further improvement” (p. 14); “A technological definition of the Industrial Revolution is a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions” (p. 16). “Useful Knowledge as an Evolving System” (draft revised February 2002, pp. 2–7): “in the past centuries useful knowledge has become a dominant factor in History” (p. 2); useful knowledge is partitioned into “propositional” knowledge, which “describes and catalogues natural phenomena and the relationships between them”, and “prescriptive” knowledge, “instructions that can be executed” (p. 5); “Inventions based on narrow epistemic bases have low adaptability and tend to lead to technological stasis fairly soon after their emergence” (p. 7). The draft says it adapts The Gifts of Athena (2002), which is unread; Khan’s review of that book (EH.Net, 2003, read in full) reports the same two categories and quotes it (p. 16): “so many scholars believe that if incentives and demand are right, somehow technology will follow automatically”. The Royal Swedish Academy’s 2025 press release (read) summarises the claim: “we not only need to know that something works, but we also need to have scientific explanations for why.” The 1999 distinction of invention from adoption is the existing strand technology/invention_adoption; this arrow adds the 2002 theory of knowledge. Its use to explain Britain’s Industrial Revolution is drawn on the debate arrow (edge_1086).

incident_edges.relationship: Coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job”: the gap needed “a better explanation than historical luck … or geographical accident”, and Pomeranz did not confront the Needham questions (2002)
incident_edges.evidence_note: “The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, author’s draft of October 2002 for the Riverside conference of November 2002 (pp. 2–4 read; draft pagination). Of coal: “Without denigrating the importance of coal or steam, the argument can be and has been overdone” (p. 2); “China’s coal reserves are immense” (p. 3). Of ghost acreage: “this argument is not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job” (p. 3). Pomeranz “does not confront the ‘Needham Questions’ squarely” (p. 4); “the sheer enormity of the gap requires a better explanation than historical luck (European discoveries) or geographical accident (coal, proximity to America)” (p. 4). The alternative he offers is the Industrial Enlightenment (p. 10), drawn on joel_mokyr → capitalismdebates (edge_1086). A draft (“little more than notes”, its title page says); no published version was read. Revision 1.146 moves this critique from edge_1050 (capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz), where revision 1.145 listed Mokyr among five named critics, to its own arrow; edge_1050 no longer names him.

incident_edges.relationship: Demand restored against the supply-side orthodoxy, which de Vries illustrates with Mokyr’s view that the Industrial Revolution’s “when,” “where” and “how fast” are “to be sought first and foremost in supply” (1977; 2008)
incident_edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, pp. 6–7, publisher excerpt, read): “Studies of modern economic growth are inevitably founded on a decisive ‘supply-side’ advance”; Adam Smith left no doubt that “The consumer responds to the developing productive forces, not the other way around”, with n. 17 quoting Mokyr’s “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” (JEH 1977, p. 1005): “The determination of ‘when,’ ‘where,’ and ‘how fast’ are to be sought first and foremost in supply, not demand-related processes”; “What began as an effort to restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (p. 7). Mokyr’s 1977 abstract (Cambridge Core, read): demand factors “were definitely of a secondary order of importance”. The 1994 article’s reference list cites the 1977 article. Qualification: de Vries cites Mokyr as an exemplar of a general orthodoxy; this is not a reply to a Mokyr text on the industrious revolution, and no reply by Mokyr was read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe's stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Vries finds differences, not 'surprising resemblances' (2009); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: This arrow represents named interventions within the debate entry, not a verdict of it; the entry includes Pomeranz and his allies, and each intervention establishes something different. Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Vries ('A World of Surprising Resemblances?', 2009, pp. 35–38, 47–48 read), on agriculture and the state: 'I would not call that a "surprising resemblance"' (p. 38); 'Coal and colonies definitely were fundamental in the Rise of the West. But reference to them cannot suffice to explain it' (p. 48). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: 'our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England'; 'Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism' (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the 'rise of the west' literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: 'The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers' (p. 958); the qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates, and moved Brenner and Isett's 2002 critique to its own arrow (robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz), as this note had foreseen. Revision 1.146 likewise moved Mokyr's 2002 critique to its own arrow (joel_mokyr → kenneth_pomeranz), since Mokyr became a person entry; the four interventions above remain.

named_group_routes.relationship: Frank's ReOrient (1998) as the polemical wing of the divergence debate: Asia central until 1800, a debate with Landes announced for December 1998 and an endorsement of Pomeranz (2001)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Notice announcing the Landes–Frank debate (Northeastern University, scheduled for 2 December 1998; read; written from Frank's side; whether the debate took place as announced is not independently confirmed): 'FRANK retorts that … Received social theory … is vitiated by the ingrained EUROCENTRISM of historiography'; Asia 'remained predominant in the world until at 1800'; 'LANDES retorts that Frank and his echoes are a magnet for fallacies and fantasies'. Frank's review of Pomeranz (JAS 2001; author's manuscript read): 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution'; Pomeranz is 'the most important … member of what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'. Mokyr (EH.Net 2012, read): 'The California School, most notably embodied in Kenneth Pomeranz's Great Divergence and Andre Gunder Frank's Re-Orient'. Vries (2013, pp. 15–16) quotes ReOrient (pp. 75, 259) and calls one passage 'a quite silly statement'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 228 n.): Beckert 'is heavily influenced by [world-systems theory's] axioms'. ReOrient itself is unread. Distinct from edge_1053 (Pomeranz → dependency).

named_group_routes.relationship: Coal in explanations of British industrialisation, as readers compare them: Mokyr places Pomeranz in a tradition “established by … E.A. Wrigley” (2002); Huang says Pomeranz simplified “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument” (2002); Clark and Jacks find that both “have made coal central to the story” (2007)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Readers’ comparisons, read. Mokyr (October 2002 draft, p. 2): Pomeranz’s coal argument “joins a venerable tradition established by Carlo Cipolla, E.A. Wrigley and others that looks at the Industrial Revolution as primarily a revolution of fossil fuel usage”. Huang (JAS 2002, pp. 532–533, read in revision 1.144): Wrigley (1988) is “a very different thing from arguing that chance, or coal, alone mattered”; Pomeranz has turned “Wrigley’s sophisticated argument that chance figured in England’s industrialization into a simple argument that coal and colonies alone mattered.” Clark and Jacks (European Review of Economic History 2007, abstract): “both E. A. Wrigley and Kenneth Pomeranz have made coal central to the story”; their coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England’s possession of coal reserves. A comparison, not an influence: no passage in which Pomeranz acknowledges Wrigley’s energy argument was read (the read pages of The Great Divergence cite Wrigley only on England’s early divergence from the continent, p. 6 n. 8). Wrigley’s argument stresses chance and the end of the organic economy; Pomeranz pairs coal with colonies.

named_group_routes.relationship: From the limits of European experience to political scale: with Rosenthal, Wong argued that European fragmentation and warfare concentrated manufacturing in cities, where higher wage costs favoured labour-saving techniques (2011, as Wong summarised in 2016 and Ma reported in 2012); in 2016 he recast divergence from “why Britain” to a more general transformation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, pp. 77–78, read): “Rosenthal and I ended up focusing on an important political difference between China and Europe – political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”; war gave “craft producers an incentive to locate in cities”; “We turned the issue of divergence from a question of why was Britain the first industrializer to why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (p. 77); “By making the question of the great divergence a more general one we recognize that even a profoundly transformative process like modern economic growth could take place in several ways and begin at several locations” (p. 78). Before and Beyond Divergence (2011) is unread; Ma’s review (EH.Net 2012, read in full in revision 1.145) reports the same dichotomy of “a unified and centralized imperial China versus a politically fragmented Europe” and the mechanism: warfare brought “a greater degree of concentration of trade and manufacturing in urban locations”, and, “With higher urban wages”, innovation in Europe “would be more biased towards saving labor than in China”. Ma finds this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter”, and the evidence on public goods “even shakier”. He also reports the authors’ challenge to “the accepted thesis of China being a high interest rate and capital scarce country”, and judges the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” for addressing “some of the key issues beyond what has been done recently by Pomeranz, Allen and others”, though “far less so when it comes to providing credible support for its own thesis”. The wage mechanism is Ma’s report; Wong’s 2016 summary gives the move of craft production to cities. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014, p. 16.2) say Rosenthal and Wong “adopted” Allen’s induced-innovation argument “wholesale”. China Transformed (1997), as Mokyr quotes it, held that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (p. 31); Mokyr objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft, pp. 3–4). The co-authored argument is Rosenthal’s as well as Wong’s.

verification.note: Expanded primary introduction check in the same later-edition preview: opening 3–4; regional-unit discussion from 7 through comparison section 10; chapter 2 household paragraph 17/note 27; chapter 6 overview from 20 through geographical-coverage conclusion 27. Intervening passages and main chapters unread; selected passages, not full introduction. Explicit resources: Wong 1997, Tilly 1984 and Mokyr 1976; Huang 1990 is a named disagreement. Quantitative historical claims not independently tested. This source remains the 2000 book, not the later 2002 exchange. Tilly title/date corroborated by publisher-supplied BiblioVault record 9780871548795; Mokyr 1976 title corroborated by journal bibliographic record. Those original books were not newly read. Addendum 2026-10-13: Whole introduction pp. 3–27 re-read in the later-edition preview (pagination of that edition), with contents pp. v–vii and index pages. Quoted for the 1.130 person entry: 'The book thus calls upon the fruits of overseas coercion to help explain the difference between European development and what we see in certain other parts of Eurasia (primarily China and Japan)—not the whole of that development'; 'Thus the book combines comparative analysis, some purely local contingency, and an integrative or global approach'; 'we have, instead, a polycentric world with no dominant center' (p. 4). 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong' (p. 7). 'truly reciprocal'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed'; 'viewing both sides of the comparison as “deviations” when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm'; n. 13: 'much more about some he does not treat extensively, such as environmental change' (p. 8). 'comparison and the analysis of connections become indistinguishable' (p. 10). Chapter 5 'offers a systematic comparison of ecological constraints in selected key areas of China and Europe'; Europe 'rescued by a combination of overseas resources and England’s breakthrough (partly conditioned by geographic good luck) in the use of subterranean stores of energy'; parallels with Sugihara Kaoru (p. 12). 'Why wasn’t England the Yangzi Delta?'; 'Europe, too, could have wound up on an “east Asian,” labor-intensive path' (p. 13). 'Constraints connected to energy, and ultimately to quantities of land (particularly the shrinking forests of core areas throughout Eurasia), were a far more important looming impediment to further growth' (p. 19). Shortages 'of fuel and building materials' in all the densest cores (p. 20). 'what was truly scarce: land and energy'; 'the fruits of overseas exploitation were probably roughly as important to at least Britain’s economic transformation as its epochal turn to fossil fuels' (p. 23). 'We end, then, with connections and interactions explaining what comparison alone cannot'; 'joining the burgeoning field of “world history,”'; 'adding a few Chinese and Japanese foils to a European story does not make it “world history.”' (p. 25). Contents: Part Three 'Beyond Smith and Malthus: From Ecological Constraints to Sustained Industrial Growth'; chapter 5 'Shared Constraints: Ecological Strain in Western Europe and East Asia' (211); chapter 6 'Abolishing the Land Constraint: The Americas as a New Kind of Periphery' (264). Huang 1990: 11–17; for a related argument see also Goldstone 1996"); labour deployment resembles "Europe’s 'industrious revolution'". (Frank 1998), p. 17 (de Vries) and the contents (p. 186, 'The Williams Thesis Revisited') re-read in the same preview.

incident_edges.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

incident_edges.relationship: Useful knowledge and the epistemic base of technique: propositional and prescriptive knowledge, macro- and microinventions, and stasis where techniques rest on “narrow epistemic bases” (1999, 2002)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, read. Editor’s introduction (1999, author-posted manuscript): “a successful macroinvention meets three criteria: novelty, workability, and potential for further improvement” (p. 14); “A technological definition of the Industrial Revolution is a clustering of macroinventions leading to an acceleration in microinventions” (p. 16). “Useful Knowledge as an Evolving System” (draft revised February 2002, pp. 2–7): “in the past centuries useful knowledge has become a dominant factor in History” (p. 2); useful knowledge is partitioned into “propositional” knowledge, which “describes and catalogues natural phenomena and the relationships between them”, and “prescriptive” knowledge, “instructions that can be executed” (p. 5); “Inventions based on narrow epistemic bases have low adaptability and tend to lead to technological stasis fairly soon after their emergence” (p. 7). The draft says it adapts The Gifts of Athena (2002), which is unread; Khan’s review of that book (EH.Net, 2003, read in full) reports the same two categories and quotes it (p. 16): “so many scholars believe that if incentives and demand are right, somehow technology will follow automatically”. The Royal Swedish Academy’s 2025 press release (read) summarises the claim: “we not only need to know that something works, but we also need to have scientific explanations for why.” The 1999 distinction of invention from adoption is the existing strand technology/invention_adoption; this arrow adds the 2002 theory of knowledge. Its use to explain Britain’s Industrial Revolution is drawn on the debate arrow (edge_1086).

incident_edges.relationship: Coal and New World land “not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job”: the gap needed “a better explanation than historical luck … or geographical accident”, and Pomeranz did not confront the Needham questions (2002)
incident_edges.evidence_note: “The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, author’s draft of October 2002 for the Riverside conference of November 2002 (pp. 2–4 read; draft pagination). Of coal: “Without denigrating the importance of coal or steam, the argument can be and has been overdone” (p. 2); “China’s coal reserves are immense” (p. 3). Of ghost acreage: “this argument is not incorrect but by itself cannot do the job” (p. 3). Pomeranz “does not confront the ‘Needham Questions’ squarely” (p. 4); “the sheer enormity of the gap requires a better explanation than historical luck (European discoveries) or geographical accident (coal, proximity to America)” (p. 4). The alternative he offers is the Industrial Enlightenment (p. 10), drawn on joel_mokyr → capitalismdebates (edge_1086). A draft (“little more than notes”, its title page says); no published version was read. Revision 1.146 moves this critique from edge_1050 (capitalismdebates → kenneth_pomeranz), where revision 1.145 listed Mokyr among five named critics, to its own arrow; edge_1050 no longer names him.

incident_edges.relationship: Demand restored against the supply-side orthodoxy, which de Vries illustrates with Mokyr’s view that the Industrial Revolution’s “when,” “where” and “how fast” are “to be sought first and foremost in supply” (1977; 2008)
incident_edges.evidence_note: The Industrious Revolution (2008, pp. 6–7, publisher excerpt, read): “Studies of modern economic growth are inevitably founded on a decisive ‘supply-side’ advance”; Adam Smith left no doubt that “The consumer responds to the developing productive forces, not the other way around”, with n. 17 quoting Mokyr’s “Demand vs. Supply in the Industrial Revolution” (JEH 1977, p. 1005): “The determination of ‘when,’ ‘where,’ and ‘how fast’ are to be sought first and foremost in supply, not demand-related processes”; “What began as an effort to restore demand as one of the cutting blades of Marshall’s supply and demand scissors” (p. 7). Mokyr’s 1977 abstract (Cambridge Core, read): demand factors “were definitely of a secondary order of importance”. The 1994 article’s reference list cites the 1977 article. Qualification: de Vries cites Mokyr as an exemplar of a general orthodoxy; this is not a reply to a Mokyr text on the industrious revolution, and no reply by Mokyr was read.
incident_edges.map_label: De Vries restores demand, citing Mokyr (2008)

incident_edges.relationship: Wrigley uses Mokyr’s two-sector calculation to illustrate why rapid growth in a small modern sector need not produce an immediate surge in aggregate growth.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own Quest (2003), 167–168, note 50, explicitly credits Mokyr’s authored editor’s introduction (1993), page 12, in his edited British Industrial Revolution. Wrigley uses the calculation for a somewhat similar purpose: hypothetical modern and traditional sectors initially comprise 10 and 90 percent and grow at 4 and 1 percent; they become equal after 74 years, with aggregate growth then 2.5 percent. This is an illustrative model, not an observed historical estimate, adoption of an entire school, or a fresh reading of Mokyr’s chapter. No independent numerical replication is claimed.
